Burren Winterage Weekend
As part of a collaborative event UNESCO Global Geopark, the 
Burren Ecotourism Network, Burrenbeo Trust and the Farming 
For Nature Programme promoted the wonderful local food from 
the Burren that has become famous for, gleaned from its fertile 
rock, sea and shore. This collaborative event showcased the best 
of the innovative Farming for Nature Programme, host-ed in the 
beautiful and inspiring location of InStone in Boston, a centre of 
excellence striving for the preservation of Cultural, Architectural, 
and Archaeological Heritage.
In attendance at the Burren Long Table Feast of local food and the 
Farming For Nature Awards on behalf of the UNESCO Global Geopark 
were Congella McGuire, Heritage Officer, Frank McCormack, Instone, 
Boston, Cllr. Joe Garrihy and Cllr. Joe Kileen.
Bridget Barry the Farming For Nature coordinator introducing the 
Farming For Nature Awards at InStone in Boston during the Burren 
Winterage Weekend.
Heritage Ireland 2030 Summit 2025 
Heritage Ireland 2030 Summit 2025: Connecting Heritage and 
Youth was held at Trinity College, Dublin (TCD) in October 2025. Keir 
McNamara of Inch Tidy Village made a presentation ‘Con-necting 
children with the local past: Mahonburgh Ringfort Conservation 
Project, Inch, Co. Clare’. Education, conservation and access work 
at Mahonburgh Ringfort is supported by Clare County Council 
and funded by the Community Monument Fund and by Heritage 
Council Community Heritage fund and was accepted under the 
Adopt a Monument Scheme in 2025. Mahonburgh Ringfort is a 
bi-vallate earthen ringfort, a homestead of a local farming group, 
built in the Iron Age and used until the Medieval period. Inch Tidy 
Village have active hands-on engagement where the community 
and the local school have participated in scrub clearance, site 
conserva-tion and making the site accessible. Future plans for the 
site include further research of the fort, placenames, biodiversity, 
bushcraft, art, promotion and awareness raising including Placed 
Based Learning, workshops, and an outdoor classroom.

Clare Schools Biodiversity Workshops 2025
387 primary and secondary school students and 22 teachers 
across County Clare have participat-ed in biodiversity workshops 
held during September and October 2025 through the ‘Clare 
Schools Biodiversity Programme’ coordinated and supported by 
Clare County Council's and supported by Creative Ireland Clare 
(Clare Libraries). This is the third year the biodiversity workshops 
have been supported by Clare County Council. Heritage in Schools 
specialists Sinead Keane and David McGrath delivered the 
biodiversity workshops. Activities included working with nature 
and art (drawing, leaf dubbing and clay modelling techniques), 
habitat identification and mapping of school grounds, installing 
bird feeders and establishing a bird monitoring programme, 
freshwater insect collecting and identification along with insect 
clay model making, identifying garden birds and pollinators, etc. 
The workshops aim to assist schools achieve their Green Flag (An 
Taisce’s Green Schools).

Clare Wetland Surveys 2025
The Clare Wetland Surveys 2025 was carried out over the 
summer months focusing on 20 sites likely to be of high 
conservation importance. Examples of wetland habitat types 
include fen, reed swamp, peatland, wet woodland, marsh and 
turloughs. The survey aims to evaluate wetland sites in terms of 
local importance, county importance, national importance and 
international im-portance and identify Annex I habitats. Three 
sites were deemed to be of National conservation value due to 
the presence of extensive areas of high quality habitat comprising 
transition mire and quaking bogs; and active raised bog (rare 
peat forming habitat). Five other sites are assessed as being of 
County conservation value (C+). The surveys have the potential 
to support local commu-nities to learn about wetland habitats in 
their locality and to link in with Community Biodiversity Action 
Plans. The study was coordinated through the Biodiversity Officer 
and is funded through the Local Biodiversity Action Fund and 
Clare County Council.

Spooky Sparks Workshop: Creating a Safe Halloween 
Experience
In collaboration with the local community, this exciting initiative is 
part of Clare County Council's effort to ensure a safer Halloween 
in the Ennis West area, blending creativity with science. Rural 
Development, through the work of the Rural and Community 
Development Officer Team was delighted to facilitate the 
workshop, which took place on October 30th, at the Cloughleigh 
Community Centre in Ennis. Experienced instructors from Craft 
Maker Spaces at Mary Immaculate College, Limerick, delivered 
the tuition event.
Designed for children aged 9 to 12 living in the Ennis West 
area, the workshop focused on the STEM program, exploring 
physics concepts like electricity and circuits through the theme 
of “designing a spooky house.” Eighteen children from the area 
participated, engaging in hands-on activities and experiments 
that enabled them to create electric lights to enhance their 
haunted creations. Funding for the event was secured from 
Creative Ireland, through the Clare Arts Officer. Additionally, 
representatives from the Gardaí and Fire Services visited the 
centre to discuss fire safety during Halloween.
Ennis Gardai and Fire Services working collaboratively with the 
community to deliver the message of a safe Halloween.

We’re Breastfeeding Friendly Clare. 
We’re Breastfeeding Friendly Clare Launch 
With support from the HSE, the We’re Breastfeeding Friendly 
Clare Booklet Relaunch, took place in the De Valera on Friday 
3rd of October as part of National Breastfeeding week 2025. The 
booklet itself was launched by Laura McHugh, the HSE National 
Breastfeeding Coordinator. Prior to launching the booklet, it was 
literacy proofed to ensure that it is presented in plain English. 
HSE Staff, members of the Healthy Clare Working Group, Clare 
libraries staff, parents and babies attended this enriching event. 
The initiative encourages businesses, organisations, and 
community spaces to adopt simple, no-cost actions that help 
mothers and families feel comfortable while breastfeeding 
in public. Research shows that a positive attitude from staff 
and acceptance from other service users are key to helping 
mothers feel at ease. Speaking at the event, Cllr Paul Murphy, 
Cathaoirleach of Clare County Council, said “This campaign is a 
collaborative effort across private, community, and statutory 
sectors. Displaying a ‘We’re Breastfeeding Friendly Clare’ sticker 
or poster shows your commitment to supporting families in a 
meaningful and important way. Local campaigns like this bring 
the Healthy Ireland Framework to life by creating supportive 
environments for families who choose to breastfeed.” 
This campaign is led out by Healthy Clare. To get involved, visit: 
https://clarecoco.ie/services/sports-recreation/healthy-clare/
breastfeedingfriendly/	
Breastfeeding Friendly Rooms Open in Ennis Health Centres. 
Following the relaunch of the We’re Breastfeeding Friendly 
booklet in Co. Clare, the HSE has opened two breastfeeding 
friendly rooms in Health Centres. These rooms have been 
designed to support mums to drop in and breastfeed in comfort. 
The rooms which are situated in Ennis Health Centre on Bindon 
Street and the new Primary Care building on Station Road are 
both open to the public from 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday. 
Speaking with Fiona and Aoife, at the opening of the room in 
Bindon Street they both said that having access to space like this 
is “fantastic.” They explained that having such rooms available so 
close to town helps to “reduce anxiety that mums can sometimes 
feel when looking for space and it also gives babies a chance to 
rest in a quiet space, which at times is all they need.” These rooms 
are also in place to support HSE staff who are returning to work, 
showing the importance that employers can play in supporting 
employee wellbeing. 
Launch of Active Ennis Water Stations 
Launch of Water Refill Stations in Tim Smyth Park 
Clare County Council’s Healthy Clare initiative, in partnership 
with Active Ennis complex, launched three water refill stations 
across the Active Ennis complex on Monday, October 13, 2025, 
as part of Clare Climate Action Week 2025. Supported by Healthy 
Ireland, the water refill stations promote the importance of 
bottle reuse, both for the environment and proper hydration in 
our daily lives. The initiative encourages individuals to remove 
plastic waste from the environment by providing the opportunity 
to refill used bottles at dedicated water stations, situated inside 
Ennis leisure facilities and positioned outside in both Tim Smythe 
Park and Lees Road. This initiative was driven by the work that 
Healthy Clare does under the programme outcome: Healthy 
Weight and current usage shows that all three stations are seeing 
high usage. This installation is expected to deliver ongoing value 
for Ennis residents, promoting good health practices through 
hydration.

Pétanque Open Day.
Pétanque Open Day.
Having previously received Healthy Clare funding for a physical 
activity programme, the KBARA committee noticed that not all 
of their members were comfortable in traditional group physical 
activity settings, noting reasons to include: fear of exercising in 
groups, poor body image, physical disability and lack of confidence 
etc. Pétanque (French Boules) was explored as a means to 
continuing group support through physical activity. The Healthy 
Clare Micro Fund, allowed for the building of the Piste and the 
purchase of materials. 30 volunteers were involved in building 
the piste and organising the Open Day. 30 members of KBARA 
were trained at Soft Opening Day for members (3 hours), 25 
members attended a talk on Pétanque and 100 people attended 
the Open Day in October. The Whats Group of Pétanque players 
has 58 members.
East Clare Community Cooperative: Yoga and 
Wellbeing. 
The project specifically targets mental health outcomes by 
promoting nervous system regulation, stress relief, emotional 
resilience, and self-care through yoga and community-based 
activities. The nature connection and being outdoors for the 
foraging element provided participants with an opportunity to 
move away from screens, into fresh air, into connection with the 
elements and the weather. Running this programme as a group 
activity addressed social integration and community connection, 
thereby reducing social isolation by creating inclusive spaces 
that bring together local residents and vulnerable groups, 
including international protection applicants, fostering stronger 
community bonds and a sense of belonging.

Cultural Companions Discover the Darker Side of 
Ennis in Afternoon Walking Tour
On the afternoon of October 22nd, Cultural Companions Clare 
hosted a memorable Dark Walking Tour of Ennis, bringing 
together 40 enthusiastic members for an engaging exploration 
of the town’s hidden history. The event began with a warm 
welcome and refreshments at the inviting Temple Gate Hotel, 
where participants gathered before setting off on their journey.
Led by the ever-popular Jane O’Brien of Ennis Walking Tours, 
the group meandered through the historic streets of Ennis, 
uncovering tales of mystery, folklore, and the town’s spookier 
past. Jane’s storytelling brought the shadows of Ennis to life, 
offering a fascinating glimpse into the lesser-known stories that 
have shaped the town’s character.
The afternoon was filled with camaraderie, curiosity, and 
laughter, as Cultural Companions continued their mission to 
create meaningful social opportunities for older adults in Clare 
through shared cultural experiences.

UKRAINIAN SERVICES TEAM 
Recent CSO figures show there were 982 Temporary Protections 
granted nationally in the past month with an average of 35 granted 
per day. There are currently 3,119 Ukrainian Beneficiaries of 
Temporary Protection (BOTP’s) living in County Clare, representing 
a decrease of 1,269 people in the County compared to figures 
released previously.  There are 912 people accommodated in 18 
multi-occupancy facilities located throughout the County - this 
reflects a decrease of 81 people compared to previous figures.  
The remaining people are accommodated in residential settings, 
in formal hosted arrangements, through the Irish Red Cross and 
Clare County Council’s Offer-a-Home scheme and other private 
arrangements. To date our Matching & Relationship Manager has 
facilitated the accommodation of 464 people that were originally 
living in hotel and multi-occupancy facilities.     
The number of younger people arriving in the Country has 
steadily increased in the last few weeks due to policy changes 
within Ukraine that allow people between the ages of 18 years 
and 22 years leave the country without facing any sanctions. 
LOCAL AUTHORITY INTEGRATION 
TEAM 
The Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) have been set up 
in all local authorities. Their purpose is to help coordinate the 
different kinds of support available for people who are applying 
for international protection, refugees, and others in similar 
situations.   
The goal of LAITs is to help IP applicants and refugees become 
independent, settle into their new communities, and participate 
in Irish life. They do this by connecting people to important 
services that can help them integrate into the community.   
Who do LAITs support?  
LAITs provide support for:  
•	
Applicants for International Protection (IP)  
•	
People who have been granted refugee status or other forms 
of protection, such as subsid-iary protection or permission 
to remain  
•	
Refugees who have been resettled in Ireland through a 
government programme  
•	
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs)  
How is the support provided?  
LAITs operate under the principle of 'Integration from Day One'. 
This means that LAITs provide integration support to people who 
need it as soon as they arrive in Ireland.  
What services do LAITs provide?  
The work of LAITs isn’t meant to replace existing services. Instead, 
LAITs help connect people with the existing services that are most 
suitable for their needs. This includes things like:  
•	
Being a direct contact for new arrivals, helping them with any 
problems they might have when dealing with public services   
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services like legal help, 
childcare and healthcare   
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services that improve their 
ability to live independently, like job training, English classes, 
education, and apprenticeships   
•	
Guiding new arrivals through the process of applying for 
financial support, medical help, child benefits, and other 
services they might need   
•	
Holding meetings in local areas and using community 
development principles to help those who attend   
•	
Supporting people if they face racism or other unfair 
treatment, helping them report it to the right authorities   
•	
Helping vulnerable new arrivals get in touch with non-
governmental organisations (NGOs) and other services if 
they need extra help

Pedestrianisation of the old Killaloe Ballina Bridge
The pedestrianisation of the Old Killaloe Ballina Bridge will 
permanently close the historic structure to vehicular traffic, 
transforming it into a dedicated pedestrian and cycling 
link between Killaloe and Ballina. This decision follows the 
conclusion of a Trial Period which began on the 27th of July and 
concluded on the 17th of October. Under the Section 38 process 
involving extensive public engagement, data collection showed 
no negative impact on traffic flow and highlighted significant 
safety and community benefits. While some opposition was 
noted, the majority of residents supported the move, citing 
improved safety for vulnerable groups, reduced pollution, and 
enhanced social and tourism opportunities. Emergency services 
confirmed their operations would not be significantly affected. 
The availability of the new Brian Boru Bridge and €90 million 
bypass now provides a viable alternative route for vehicles, 
enabling this long-considered change. Both Tipperary County 
Council and Clare County Council have pledged ongoing support 
for local businesses and aim to position the pedestrianised 
bridge as a central feature of the area’s tourism appeal.

Local Enterprise Office Clare piloted a hands-on, 5-part online

event’s taster menu, including St. Tola Cheese, Linalla Ice Cream,

Digital Skills Training for Seniors in Ennistymon 
Digital Hub
The Digital Transformation Department are currently running a 
Digital Skills Training initiative, which pairs seniors with Transition 
Year students from Ennistymon Community School to build 
essential technology skills. The aim of the training is to strengthen 
digital inclusion and promote community engagement.
The program covers topics such as Internet browsing and 
searching, email setup and usage, WhatsApp communication, 
social media and how to stay safe online. Feedback from 
participants has been overwhelmingly positive, with many 
expressing how valuable it is to have patient, one-on-one support 
from the students.
The intergenerational aspect of the program has been a 
highlight. Participants appreciate the social interaction and 
confidence boost, while students are gaining communication 
skills and enjoying the opportunity to learn from participants’ 
life experiences. Each session runs for 90 minutes followed by 
tea/coffee and biscuits which has been a great opportunity for 
conversation and connection.
